title: Mutation operators and equivalent mutants
summary: The changes Stryker.NET makes (equality, arithmetic, logical, boolean, string, LINQ, statement and block removal, null coalescing), mutants no test can kill, and tests that kill LINQ mutants.

steps.title: What a mutation tool changes
body: Stryker.NET (the standard mutation tool for .NET, version 4.x/5.x) rewrites your code with **mutators**, each modelling a common slip:
| Statement / block removal | a method call or a whole block deleted |
Each mutant ends as **Killed**, **Survived**, **Timeout** (counted as caught), **NoCoverage** (no test even runs it), **CompileError** or **Ignored** (filtered out by configuration).

Some mutants **cannot** be killed because they do not change behaviour: an **equivalent mutant**. Example: `for (var i = 0; i < list.Count; i++)` → `i != list.Count`. For a loop that only counts up by one, both stop at the same place. Do not twist tests to kill those; mark them in the code with a reason (`// Stryker disable once Equality : equivalent, i only counts up by 1`) or accept a score a little below 100%.

steps.prompt: Match each mutant to its mutator.
Which mutant of `public static int Clamp(int x) => x < 0 ? 0 : x;` is **equivalent** (no test can kill it)?
steps.explain: When x is 0, the original returns x (0) and the mutant returns 0: the same value for every input. The others change the result for some input, so a test can kill them.

steps.title: Kill the LINQ mutants
prompt: Blog posts carry tags typed by authors. The normaliser, compiled beside your tests:
// Trimmed and lower-case; blanks and nulls dropped; duplicates removed (first one wins, order kept); at most 5.

Write `public class TagsTests` with at least **4** tests that compare whole lists (`Assert.Equal(new[] { ... }, result)`). Six planted bugs, the kind Stryker makes: a LINQ call removed or swapped, the filter loosened, a string call removed.
solution: public void Trims_and_lower_cases() => Assert.Equal(new[] { "dotnet", "testing" }, Tags.Normalize([" DotNet ", "Testing"]));
public void Drops_blanks_and_nulls() => Assert.Equal(new[] { "api" }, Tags.Normalize(["", "   ", null, "api"]));

mutants.name: LINQ: sorted instead of first-seen order
mutants.hint: Use tags whose first-seen order is not alphabetical.

mutants.name: String: upper case instead of lower

hints: One test per rule in the comment: trim and case, blanks and nulls, duplicates, the limit of five.
The duplicates test should keep a non-alphabetical order, such as `xunit` before `csharp`, so a sorting bug shows.
The limit test needs more than five tags, and expects exactly the first five.
steps.explain: Comparing whole lists kills every LINQ mutant at once: order, count and content all show in one assertion, and xUnit's message points at the first position that differs.
